# Peaking and tapering in an in-season college football schedule
## 1. The question

-As asked: how should we peak and taper for in-season college football? In practice it splits into four questions. What does a normal game week look like as a small taper? How long does each quality last without exposure, so what has to be touched every week? How should Applied Performance read readiness in game week? What do we do in the few windows with no game: bye weeks, camp to week 1, and the postseason gap?

+As asked: how should we peak and taper for in-season college football? It splits four ways: what a normal game week looks like as a small taper; how long each quality lasts without exposure; how to read readiness in game week; and what to do in game-free windows (bye weeks, camp to week 1, the postseason gap).

-The sources mostly answer a different question. Every peaking model in the library was built on single-event or discrete-meet sports: kayakers ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]] [supported]), one swimmer ([[block-periodization--issurin/case-study--popov-competition-shortens-residual-effects]] [untested]), throwers ([[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] [supported]). Football plays 12 or more weekly games and has no single peak. **External:** Pyne, Mujika and Reilly 2009 (abstract) say taper research is concentrated in individual sports and single events and does not yet guide a team's league season. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 5) call sustaining a peak across a long season unrealistic. The evidence ceiling is low: no study in two periodization meta-analyses tested whether adaptations peaked when a model predicted ([[research-papers/afonso-2019-a-systematic-review-of-meta-analyses-comparing-periodized-and-non-periodized-exercise-prog]], paper brief, pp. 1, 4). So this note treats the season as "hold readiness every week" and keeps "peak on purpose" for the rare game-free window.

+The sources mostly answer a different question. Every peaking model in the library comes from individual-event sports (kayak, swimming, track and field). **External:** Pyne, Mujika and Reilly 2009 (abstract) say taper research centres on individual sports and single events and does not yet guide a team's league season. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 5) call sustaining a peak across a long season unrealistic. No study in two periodization meta-analyses tested whether adaptations peaked when a model predicted ([[research-papers/afonso-2019-a-systematic-review-of-meta-analyses-comparing-periodized-and-non-periodized-exercise-prog|Afonso 2019]], pp. 1, 4). So this note treats the season as "hold readiness every week" and keeps "peak on purpose" for the rare game-free window.
## 2. Bottom line
-1. Keep a floor of one heavy lower-body strength session every game week, early in the week, with load kept high and sets cut. [supported direction; floor, not optimum; no football trial]

-2. Give every player one true max-velocity exposure every game week, planned rather than assumed from practice, with priority on positions that rarely reach top speed in games. [contested on the day count, supported on direction]

-3. Shape the week heavy-early and light-late: heaviest lifting and practice Tuesday and Wednesday, at least 48 h between the last heavy or high-volume session and kickoff, and cut volume, not intensity, from Thursday on. [supported for the shape; descriptive only in college football]

-4. Read game-week readiness from CMJ strategy metrics (mRSI or RSImod, flight time to contraction time), no arm swing, against each player's own norm and split by position group and starter status. Do not rely on jump height alone or on ACWR. [supported direction; football samples are small]

-5. Save a real multi-day taper (about 1 to 2 weeks, volume cut about 40 to 60%, intensity kept) for one planned peak after a game-free gap, such as a bowl. [supported in other sports; untested in football]

+1. Every game week has two floors: one heavy lower-body session, load high and sets cut [supported direction; the tested minimum, not Issurin's two-session template; no football trial], and one planned max-velocity exposure for every player [contested; no football data]. Inference: prioritize positions that rarely reach top speed in games (no source tests this).

+2. Lift heaviest early in the week; for a Saturday game, hold the last high-volume practice no later than Wednesday and cut volume, not intensity, from Thursday. [Issurin's template (rugby league, Baker 2001) and one D-I program agree on early-heavy, late-light; they differ on the heaviest practice day; descriptive only in college football] Inference: keep about 48 h between the last heavy or high-volume session and kickoff, drawn from Verkhoshansky's 48 h recovery after high-CNS work and Pritchard 2015's 2 to 4 days of cessation before a strength peak; no source tests a gap to kickoff.

+3. Read game-week readiness from CMJ strategy metrics (mRSI or RSImod, FT:CT), no arm swing, against each player's own norm, not from jump height alone or ACWR. These metrics are noisier than jump height, so set thresholds from each player's typical error. [supported direction; football samples are small] Inference: splitting by position group and starter status rests on off-season profiles and one exploratory study; no source sets game-week thresholds by group.
+4. Keep aerobic and repeat-effort conditioning in every week; it may be the quality lost fastest. [contested: Eric's baseline and Mujika and Padilla 2000 against Issurin's table]

+5. Save a real multi-day taper (about 1 to 3 weeks, volume cut about 40 to 60%, intensity kept) for one planned peak after a game-free gap, such as a bowl. [supported in other sports; untested in football]
## 3. Where the sources agree

-**Cut volume, keep intensity.** Issurin's pre-competitive microcycle cuts total and intense volume, keeps session frequency, and raises the share of max-speed and sport-specific work ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] [supported], PDF p. 105). Bondarchuk keeps strength exercises "to a somewhat lesser volume to maintain the achieved level" ([[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] [supported], PDF p. 175; track and field). **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003 (abstract): keep intensity, cut volume up to 60 to 90%, cut frequency no more than 20%. **External:** Bosquet et al. 2007 (abstract; 27 studies, mostly endurance): a 2-week taper with volume cut 41 to 60% and no change in intensity or frequency was most efficient. **External:** Pritchard et al. 2019 (abstract; crossover, 11 strength-trained men, not in season): only the higher-intensity taper improved IMTP relative peak force and CMJ FT:CT.

+**Cut volume, keep intensity.** Issurin's pre-competitive microcycle cuts total and intense volume, keeps session frequency, and raises the share of max-speed and sport-specific work ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning|Issurin pre-competitive]] [supported], PDF p. 105). **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003 (abstract): keep intensity, cut volume up to 60 to 90%, cut frequency no more than 20%. **External:** Bosquet et al. 2007 (abstract; 27 studies; sports not listed in the abstract, mostly endurance per the evidence file): a 2-week taper with volume cut 41 to 60% and no change in intensity or frequency was most efficient. **External:** Pritchard et al. 2019 (abstract; crossover, 11 strength-trained men, 1-week taper, about 70% volume cut): the tapers did not differ significantly; only the higher-intensity taper showed small effect-size gains in IMTP relative peak force and CMJ FT:CT.

-**Strength lasts; speed is fragile.** Issurin lists max strength at 30 ± 5 days and alactic speed at 5 ± 3 days after training stops, with no sample reported ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]] [contested], PDF p. 35). He grounds speed's short residual in "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions" (same entry, PDF pp. 35-36). Issurin, citing Fleck and Kraemer 1997, says team-sport players hold strength near pre-season for 14 to 16 weeks, then lose it sharply ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-109; secondhand, the only in-season figure in the library). **External:** Ronnestad et al. 2011 (abstract; professional soccer, n = 7 per group): one session per week kept strength and 40-m sprint for 12 weeks; one session every two weeks lost both. **External:** Spiering et al. 2021 (abstract; mostly general and younger adult populations): strength held up to 32 weeks on one session and one set per exercise per week if relative load was kept; the authors say data are too thin for athlete-specific advice. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 3): games give some stimulus but likely not enough to keep max speed.

+**Strength holds on a small dose.** Issurin, citing Fleck and Kraemer 1997, says team-sport players hold strength near pre-season for 14 to 16 weeks, then lose it sharply ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle|Issurin in-season week]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-109; secondhand). **External:** Ronnestad et al. 2011 (abstract; professional soccer, n = 7 per group): one session per week kept strength and 40-m sprint for 12 weeks; one every two weeks lost both; jump height did not change in either group. **External:** Spiering et al. 2021 (abstract; mostly younger general adults) found strength held up to 32 weeks on one set per exercise per week at kept relative load, but say the data are too thin for athlete advice.

-**Heavy early, light late.** Issurin, citing Baker 2001 (one rugby league study), splits the in-season week into an early strength mini-block and a late practice mini-block, with 28 to 30 h between the last strength key-workout and the key practice ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-111). Inference: the worked week assumes a Sunday game, so a Saturday game moves it one day earlier. Low-frequency peripheral fatigue can last up to 48 h ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]] [supported], printed p. 15), and high volume just before competition may hurt ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] [supported], PDF pp. 99-100). College data match the shape. **External:** Wellman et al. 2019 (Zotero; 31 D-I players, one program): Tuesday was the planned high-load day, and in weeks 9 to 12 Tuesday and Wednesday loads fell by a preplanned cut in duration while Thursday did not change (PDF p. 6). Lewis (dissertation, year unverified; Zotero PDF p. 86) found Tuesday and Wednesday practices came closest to game demands for linemen.

+**Heavy early, light late.** Issurin, citing Baker 2001 (one rugby league study), splits the week into an early strength mini-block and a late practice mini-block. For a Sunday game: strength key-workouts Tuesday and Wednesday mornings, the week's key practice ("substantial or big" load) Thursday afternoon, 28 to 30 h after the last lift, and only the pre-game session load-restricted (same entry, PDF pp. 108-111). Inference: shifting one day earlier for a Saturday game gives lifts Monday and Tuesday mornings, key practice Wednesday afternoon, Thursday off, a light Friday. High volume just before competition may hurt ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing|Verkhoshansky taper timing]] [supported], PDF pp. 99-100). **External:** Wellman et al. 2019 (Zotero; 31 D-I players, one program, PDF p. 6): in weeks 9 to 12 Tuesday and Wednesday loads fell by a preplanned duration cut while Thursday did not change.

-**Fast force stays down for 3 to 4 days after a game.** After a soccer match, hamstring RTD and sprint time were still impaired at 72 h ([[research-papers/cosio-2026-transcriptomic-profiling-of-the-biceps-femoris-long-head-72-h-following-a-football-match-a]], paper brief, p. 8; n = 9 regional players). After AFL matches, early RFD (0 to 50 ms) was still down at 96 h while peak force barely moved, and the responsive metric was the noisiest (CV 16.4%) ([[research-papers/norris-2019-recovery-of-forcetime-characteristics-after-australian-rules-football-matches-examining-th]], paper brief, p. 2).

+**Strategy metrics beat output metrics.** In D-I football, jump height fell only slightly by 24 h after training while RSImod and FT:CT stayed largely reduced ([[research-papers/lewis-undated-athlete-monitoring-in-american-collegiate-football|Lewis]], pp. 96-97; n = 5). At 72 h after intermittent running, flight time moved -0.7% while FT:CT fell 7.7% ([[research-papers/gathercole-2015-alternative-countermovement-jump-analysis-to-quantify-acute-neuromuscular-fatigue|Gathercole 2015]], p. 7; n = 8). The cost is noise: several phase-duration and RFD variables failed reliability, FT:CT was less reliable with arm swing, and the study tested reliability, not sensitivity ([[research-papers/heishman-2020-countermovement-jump-reliability-performed-with-and-without-an-arm-swing-in-ncaa-division|Heishman 2020]], pp. 5-12; D-I basketball). ACWR offered no predictive advantage over an intercept-only model ([[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor|Impellizzeri 2020]], pp. 4-5).

-**Strategy metrics beat output metrics.** In D-I football, jump height recovered by 24 h after training while RSImod and FT:CT stayed down ([[research-papers/lewis-undated-athlete-monitoring-in-american-collegiate-football]], paper brief, pp. 96-97; n = 5 per CMJ study). At 72 h after intermittent running, flight time moved -0.7% while FT:CT fell 7.7% ([[research-papers/gathercole-2015-alternative-countermovement-jump-analysis-to-quantify-acute-neuromuscular-fatigue]], paper brief, p. 7; n = 8). No-arm-swing CMJ suits acute readiness ([[research-papers/heishman-2020-countermovement-jump-reliability-performed-with-and-without-an-arm-swing-in-ncaa-division]], paper brief, pp. 5-12; D-I basketball). ACWR offered no predictive advantage over an intercept-only model, leaving only "not too much too soon" ([[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor]], paper brief, pp. 4-5).
## 4. Where they disagree

-**Which quality is lost first (D-6).** Three positions. Issurin: speed goes first, aerobic and strength last ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]] [contested]). Eric's class-4 slides: aerobic goes first, speed last (section 7). **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2000 Part I (abstract): under 4 weeks of reduced stimulus, highly trained athletes lose VO2max fast while strength losses are limited, which sides with class 4 on aerobic. **External:** Saldanha et al. 2026 (abstract; 17 to 21 semi-professional soccer players, uncontrolled): after a 5-day break, max velocity and repeated-sprint time got worse while jump and thigh strength held, which sides with Issurin on speed. **External:** Ross and Leveritt 2001 (Zotero, PDF p. 17): short-sprint losses are milder than expected, longer sprints suffer more. Inference: these may answer different questions (loss after full cessation versus loss under a small retention dose), so they should not be merged yet. What would settle it: our own sprint and CMJ data before and after bye weeks and winter break.

+**Where the heaviest practice sits, and the post-game window.** Issurin puts the key practice late (Wednesday after the Saturday shift). College data put it early: Wellman's program planned Tuesday as the highest practice load (PDF p. 6), and Lewis (dissertation, year unverified; PDF p. 86) found Tuesday and Wednesday practices closest to game demands for linemen. Both sit inside the post-game window. After AFL matches, early IMTP RFD (0 to 50 ms) was still down 17.8% at 72 h and 16.9% at 96 h while peak force barely moved, CV 16.4% ([[research-papers/norris-2019-recovery-of-forcetime-characteristics-after-australian-rules-football-matches-examining-th|Norris 2019]], p. 2). After a soccer match, hamstring RTD and sprint time were still impaired at 72 h ([[research-papers/cosio-2026-transcriptomic-profiling-of-the-biceps-femoris-long-head-72-h-following-a-football-match-a|Cosio 2026]], p. 8; n = 9, no control group). A Saturday game puts Monday at about 48 h, Tuesday about 72 h, Wednesday about 96 h. Unresolved: either the early-week lifts and practice load incompletely recovered players by design (Issurin's model), or heavy and high-velocity work waits until Wednesday. No source tests this in football. What would settle it: our CMJ and sprint data by hours since the game.

-**Heavy lifting close to competition (D-5, D-7).** Issurin reports both sides: Platonov and Fesenko 1990 (swimmers, volleyball, tennis) say heavy work before competition hurts technique; Bompa and Carrera 2003 say sport-specific strength work keeps the force component ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] [supported], PDF p. 108). **External:** Pritchard et al. 2015 (abstract; strength athletes): 2 to 4 days without lifting appears best for peak max strength. Inference: in a Saturday week that puts the last heavy lift on Tuesday or Wednesday. What would settle it: mRSI on game-day minus 1 by days since the last heavy lift.

+**Which quality is lost first (D-6).** Issurin's table: speed goes first (5 ± 3 days), aerobic and max strength last (30 ± 5), no sample reported, grounded in "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions" ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability|Issurin residuals]] [contested], PDF pp. 35-36). **Eric's baseline (class-4-2026 slides, p. 47):** aerobic goes first, speed last. **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2000 Part I (abstract): under 4 weeks of reduced stimulus, highly trained athletes lose VO2max fast while strength losses are limited. Inference: this sides with class 4 on aerobic. The residual entry adds that intense work does not prevent aerobic detraining during a taper (Mujika 1999, PDF p. 34). **External:** Saldanha et al. 2026 (abstract; 17 to 21 semi-professional soccer players, uncontrolled): after a 5-day break, repeated-sprint time and RAST peak velocity worsened (small to moderate) while jump and hip adductor and abductor strength held. Inference: this leans toward Issurin on speed, though RAST is not a max-velocity test. Against a short speed residual: **External:** Ross and Leveritt 2001 (Zotero, PDF p. 17): short-sprint detraining is "less severe than may have been reasonably anticipated"; longer sprints suffer more. **External:** Bosquet et al. 2013 (abstract; meta-analysis, 103 studies, mixed populations): cessation cut maximal power least (SMD -0.20, against -0.46 for maximal force). Ronnestad (above) kept 40-m speed without dedicated max-velocity work. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 3) say games likely do not keep max speed, but cite Issurin for it. Inference, which the residual entry itself flags: these may answer different questions (full cessation versus a small retention dose). Issurin warns that a design built only on residual lengths "will be extremely rigid and inflexible" ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks|Issurin residual mini-blocks]] [supported], PDF p. 127). What would settle it: our sprint and CMJ data before and after bye weeks and winter break.

-**Maintain or build in season.** Ronnestad and Spiering say one session per week maintains. **External:** Hoffman et al. 2003 (abstract; freshman players, n = 14 per group, two separate seasons, 2 sessions per week): a linear in-season program raised 1RM squat by 13.8 ± 7.4 kg while the nonlinear one did not; the abstract garbles the second program, so verify the full text. Inference: building may be realistic for low-snap freshmen, not starters.

+**Heavy lifting close to competition (D-5, D-7).** Issurin reports both sides: Platonov and Fesenko 1990 say heavy work before competition hurts technique; Bompa and Carrera 2003 say sport-specific strength work keeps the force component (Issurin pre-competitive, PDF p. 108). **External:** Pritchard et al. 2015 (abstract; strength athletes): 2 to 4 days of training cessation appears optimal for peak max strength. Inference: a football week never stops training, so this bounds the last heavy lift rather than setting it; the shifted Issurin week puts it about 4 days out. What would settle it: mRSI on game-day minus 1 by days since the last heavy lift.

-**Timing models (D-1, D-2).** Bompa's supercompensation windows ([[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] [supported], Ch 1) against Verkhoshansky's adaptive reconstruction, where timing "remains indeterminate" ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] [contested], PDF pp. 94-99), and Evans calling the fitness-fatigue model "JUST A CONCEPT" ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept]] [untested]). Inference: use them as mental models; do not schedule to the hour.

+**Maintain or build in season.** **External:** Ronnestad and Spiering (above) say one session per week maintains; Issurin's template uses two. **External:** Hoffman et al. 2003 (abstract; freshman players, n = 14 per group, two separate seasons, 2 sessions per week): a linear in-season program raised 1RM squat by 13.8 ± 7.4 kg while the nonlinear one did not; the abstract garbles the second program, so verify the full text. Inference: building may be realistic for low-snap freshmen, not starters.

+**Timing models (D-1, D-2).** Bompa ([[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle|Bompa supercompensation]] [supported], Ch 1), Verkhoshansky ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation|Verkhoshansky adaptive reconstruction]] [contested], PDF pp. 94-99) and Evans ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept|Evans fitness-fatigue]] [untested]) disagree on whether adaptation timing can be predicted. Inference: use them as mental models; do not schedule to the hour.
## 5. What transfers and what does not

-**Transfers:** the direction of residual effects and a weekly re-exposure cadence for speed; the in-season two-mini-block week; keep intensity, cut volume; readiness monitoring with CMJ strategy metrics; the 72 to 96 h post-game window for fast-force work. Also that body mass is not a taper marker: fat mass rose 4.3% over a 2-week taper with stable body mass ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]] [supported], PDF pp. 126-127; the primary abstract shows n = 16). Inference: linemen with high intake in a low-load window are most exposed.

+**Transfers:** the direction of residual effects and a weekly re-exposure cadence; the two-mini-block week as a template; keep intensity, cut volume; CMJ strategy metrics. Also that body mass is not a taper marker: fat mass rose 4.3% over a 2-week taper at stable body mass ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription|Issurin realization taper]] [supported], PDF pp. 126-127; triathletes, n = 16, no significance test reported). Inference: linemen with high intake in a low-load window are most exposed.

-**Does not transfer:** single-peak taper prescriptions. Issurin's 1 to 3 week realization block, the kayak race-simulation dosage, the 8 to 10 sessions per week camp figure, Bompa's 4 to 12 week delayed gain after concentrated loading ([[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]] [supported], Ch 2), and the roughly 3% taper gain (**External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003, abstract) all assume one target event. A game week has no room for them.

+**Does not transfer:** single-peak prescriptions (Issurin's 1 to 3 week realization block, kayak dosages, 8 to 10 sessions per week, the 4 to 12 week delayed gain after concentrated loading (Siff and Verkhoshansky, cited by Bompa: [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching|Bompa concentrated loading]] [supported], Ch 2), the roughly 3% taper gain in Mujika and Padilla 2003) assume one target event.

-**The exception:** one planned peak after game-free weeks, such as a bowl or a title game with a gap. **External:** Marrier et al. 2017 (Zotero abstract only; 10 international rugby sevens players, 3-week taper after a 4-week camp): 70 to 80% of individual peaks fell in the first 2 weeks. **External:** Vachon et al. 2021 (abstract; 14 team-sport studies): tapering gave moderate gains in power, change of direction and VO2max, but the studies could not say which strategy is best. **External:** Haugen et al. 2019 (PDF p. 11): sprinters should expect smaller taper gains than endurance or strength athletes. Inference: for a bowl, run 1 to 2 weeks of reduced volume with speed and heavy lifting kept, and do not judge success from sprint times alone.

+**The exception:** one planned peak after game-free weeks, such as a bowl. **External:** Marrier et al. 2017 (Zotero abstract only; 10 international rugby sevens players, 3-week taper after a 4-week camp): 70 to 80% of individual peaks fell in the first 2 weeks. **External:** Vachon et al. 2021 (abstract; 14 team-sport studies): tapering gave moderate gains in power, change of direction and VO2max, but no best strategy emerged. **External:** Haugen et al. 2019 (PDF p. 11): 2 to 3 weeks for strength and power sports, with smaller gains expected in sprinters. Fitness-fatigue modelling suggests accepted tapers "may be too rigorous and short" (Fitz-Clarke 1991, in Verkhoshansky taper timing, printed pp. 88-89). Inference: for a bowl, run 1 to 3 weeks of reduced volume with speed and heavy lifting kept, and do not judge success from sprint times alone.
## 6. What none of them covers

-- **Bye weeks.** No source prescribes one. Peterson (dissertation, grey literature, year and institution unverified; 108 D-I players, 2021 to 2023) found skill and mid-size players jumped better after the bye than at baseline while big players jumped worse, and the gap lasted to 24 h after the next game (PDF p. 52, Table 6). Inference: a bye may need position-specific dosing, and should still include one speed and one heavy exposure given Saldanha.

-- **Short weeks.** Only soccer load-ratio data, descriptive ([[research-papers/galiano-2026-more-matches-less-time-how-load-ratios-reveal-gaps-between-training-and-competition-in-foo]], paper brief, pp. 4-5).

-- **Camp to week 1.** Wellman describes a deliberate duration cut in week 1 (PDF p. 6); the closest intervention is U17 futsal, n = 9 per group ([[research-papers/claudino-2016-autoregulating-jump-performance-to-induce-functional-overreaching]], paper brief).

-- **Postseason and the bowl gap.** All bowl-prep structure is Inference from kayak calendars. Nothing covers a title game followed by an uncertain bowl date or consecutive playoff games. For a long layoff, contact should rebuild over at least 3 to 4 weeks and high-speed running progressively ([[research-papers/stokes-2020-returning-to-play-after-prolonged-training-restrictions-in-professional-collision-sports]], paper brief, p. 7; expert opinion, rugby).

-- **Position groups.** CMJ profiles differ by group ([[research-papers/merrigan-2022-comparisons-of-countermovement-jump-force-time-characteristics-among-national-collegiate-a]], paper brief; off-season data) and game load differs by exposure ([[research-papers/lever-2026-game-exposure-shapes-intensity-and-performance-in-division-i-college-football]], paper brief). Nothing says how dose should differ.

-- **Low-snap players.** Non-starters showed poorer recovery markers despite lower external load ([[research-papers/aychman-2026-multimodal-indicators-of-non-functional-overreaching-in-ncaa-division-i-american-football]], paper brief, pp. 1, 9; 39 players, one program, exploratory). No source prescribes make-up loading.
-- **Detraining across a football season.** Only the secondhand 14 to 16 week figure.

+- **Bye weeks.** No source prescribes one. **External:** Peterson (dissertation, grey literature, year and institution unverified; 108 D-I players, 2021 to 2023) found a group x time interaction on a CMJ stretch-shortening factor: the gap between big players and skill or mid-size players widened after the bye and persisted 24 h after the next game (PDF p. 52, Table 6). Within-group change from baseline is not tested on that page. Inference: a bye may need position-specific dosing and should still include a speed or repeated-sprint exposure, given Saldanha.

+- **Short weeks, camp to week 1, position groups, low-snap players.** Evidence is descriptive or off-population: soccer load ratios ([[research-papers/galiano-2026-more-matches-less-time-how-load-ratios-reveal-gaps-between-training-and-competition-in-foo|Galiano 2026]], pp. 4-5); Wellman's week-1 duration cut (PDF p. 6); U17 futsal, n = 9 per group ([[research-papers/claudino-2016-autoregulating-jump-performance-to-induce-functional-overreaching|Claudino 2016]]); off-season CMJ profiles by position ([[research-papers/merrigan-2022-comparisons-of-countermovement-jump-force-time-characteristics-among-national-collegiate-a|Merrigan 2022]]); game load by exposure ([[research-papers/lever-2026-game-exposure-shapes-intensity-and-performance-in-division-i-college-football|Lever 2026]]); non-starters with poorer recovery despite lower load ([[research-papers/aychman-2026-multimodal-indicators-of-non-functional-overreaching-in-ncaa-division-i-american-football|Aychman 2026]], pp. 1, 9; one program, exploratory). None says how dose should differ.

+- **Postseason, the bowl gap, consecutive playoff games.** Bowl structure is Inference from kayak calendars. After a long layoff, contact should rebuild over at least 3 to 4 weeks ([[research-papers/stokes-2020-returning-to-play-after-prolonged-training-restrictions-in-professional-collision-sports|Stokes 2020]], p. 7; expert opinion, rugby).
+- **Detraining across a season.** Only the secondhand 14 to 16 week figure and one in-season freshman strength study (Hoffman 2003); nothing on starters' speed or strength across a season.

-Would help: Bompa Ch 7 "Peaking for Competition" (printed pp. 187-202) and Ch 5 and 8; Issurin Ch 4; Fullagar et al. 2017 full text (stub only); text extraction for Marrier 2017. The NCAA in-season limit of 20 countable hours per week comes only from secondary compliance pages and must be checked against the current D-I Manual.
+Would fill these: Bompa Ch 7 "Peaking for Competition" and Issurin Ch 4; the rest are listed in the evidence map, Gaps.
## 7. Eric's baseline

-- **Eric's baseline:** mRSI from daily CMJ is the daily readiness marker, chosen over wellness surveys because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable" (method-baseline, SportSmith piece). Daily wellness surveys were dropped after about one year because athletes learned to game them. This agrees with section 3 on strategy metrics and with [[research-papers/mccall-2023-a-qualitative-study-of-11-world-class-team-sport-athletes-experiences-answering-subjective]] (paper brief) on honest answering being a trust problem.
-- **Eric's baseline (class-4-2026 slides, p. 47):** aerobic traits are lost fastest and alactic or speed traits slowest, and that order sets re-exposure frequency. This conflicts with Issurin.

-- **Course baseline (HHPR 5355, speaker unconfirmed):** speed needs re-exposure about every 5 days and aerobic capacity and max strength about every 30 (class-1 transcript p. 27). This matches Issurin and conflicts with the class-4 slide.

-- **Course baseline (HHPR 5355, speaker unconfirmed):** in season, "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (class-1 pp. 20-21; class-8 slides p. 21); strength keeps a minimal retention dose inside its roughly 30-day window (pp. 24-25); in-season volume and intensity are waved to avoid monotony (p. 21); a training week need not be 7 days (pp. 17-18). All agree with section 3.

-- **Eric's baseline (class-4 slides, pp. 34, 39):** football conditioning targets alactic and aerobic capacity; glycolytic work is absorbed through camp and practice. This fits the 1:7 work-to-rest ratio of D-I games ([[research-papers/iosia-2008-analysis-of-exercise-to-rest-ratios-during-division-ia-televised-football-competition]], paper brief; 2004 data).
-- The first-person preference for undulating over linear periodization sits in the same unreliably diarized transcript and is unconfirmed as Eric's (baseline tension 9).

+- **Eric's baseline:** mRSI from daily CMJ is the readiness marker, chosen over wellness surveys as "objective, consistent, and actionable" (method-baseline, SportSmith piece); surveys were dropped after about a year because athletes gamed them. Inference: this agrees with section 3 and with [[research-papers/mccall-2023-a-qualitative-study-of-11-world-class-team-sport-athletes-experiences-answering-subjective|McCall 2023]] on honest answering as a trust problem.
+- **Eric's baseline (class-4-2026 slides, p. 47):** aerobic traits are lost fastest and speed slowest, and that order sets re-exposure frequency. This conflicts with Issurin's table.

+- **Course baseline (HHPR 5355, speaker unconfirmed):** speed needs re-exposure about every 5 days, aerobic capacity and max strength about every 30 (class-1 transcript p. 27). These numbers are Issurin's Table 1.6 reproduced in the course slides (week1-lecture p. 66), not independent support, and the same transcript says aerobic capacity is gained and lost quickly (pp. 25, 28). The one real disagreement is class-4 p. 47 against Issurin's table.

+- **Course baseline (HHPR 5355, speaker unconfirmed):** in season, "maintain intensity, reduce volume", a minimal strength retention dose, waved volume and intensity, and weeks not tied to 7 days (class-1 pp. 17-25; class-8 slides p. 21). All agree with section 3.

+- **Eric's baseline (class-4 slides, pp. 34, 39):** football conditioning targets alactic and aerobic capacity; glycolytic work is absorbed through camp and practice. Inference: this fits the roughly 1:7 ratio in 2004 D-I games ([[research-papers/iosia-2008-analysis-of-exercise-to-rest-ratios-during-division-ia-televised-football-competition|Iosia 2008]]).
+- The first-person preference for undulating over linear periodization is unconfirmed as Eric's (baseline tension 9).
## 8. Questions for Eric
1. In a 12-plus game season, what does "peak" mean for us: every Saturday at the same level, specific target games, or only the postseason?
-2. How are bye weeks used now: restoration, a loading block, or a speed and strength top-up? Does it differ by position group?

-3. Your class-4 slide (p. 47) says aerobic is lost fastest and speed slowest; the class-1 transcript (p. 27) says speed needs re-exposure about every 5 days, as Issurin does. Which is your view, and is the difference cessation versus a retention dose?
-4. Are the course-baseline in-season rules yours (maintain intensity and reduce volume, a 30-day strength retention dose, a 5-day speed cadence, waving the week)?
-5. How should Applied Performance read readiness in game week: which mRSI drop, on which day, triggers a change, and do linemen and low-snap players get separate thresholds?
-6. Does the postseason get a distinct taper (1 to 2 weeks, volume down, intensity kept) or the normal game-week template?

+2. In a Saturday week, where do the heaviest lifts and the heaviest practice sit now? Issurin's shifted week lifts Monday and Tuesday, about 48 and 72 h after the game, when soccer and AFL data show fast force still down. Is lifting on incompletely recovered players deliberate, or should heavy and high-velocity work wait until Wednesday?

+3. Your class-4 slide (p. 47) says aerobic is lost fastest and speed slowest. The course's 5 and 30 day figures are Issurin's table, and class-1 also says aerobic is gained and lost quickly. Is class-4 your view, and are the other course in-season rules yours (maintain intensity, reduce volume, a strength retention dose, a waved week)?
+4. How are bye weeks used now: restoration, a loading block, or a speed and strength top-up? Does it differ by position group?
+5. Which mRSI drop, on which day, triggers a change in game week, and do linemen and low-snap players get separate thresholds?
+6. Does the postseason get a distinct taper (1 to 3 weeks, volume down, intensity kept) or the normal game-week template?
## 9. Sources used

-Library entries (confidence): [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]] [supported]; [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] [supported]; [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]] [contested]; [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] [supported]; [[block-periodization--issurin/case-study--popov-competition-shortens-residual-effects]] [untested]; [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] [supported]; [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]] [supported]; [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] [supported]; [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] [contested]; [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] [supported]; [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]] [supported]; [[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept]] [untested].

+Library entries (confidence): [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription|Issurin realization taper]] [supported]; [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning|Issurin pre-competitive]] [supported]; [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability|Issurin residuals]] [contested]; [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle|Issurin in-season week]] [supported]; [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks|Issurin residual mini-blocks]] [supported]; [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms|Verkhoshansky fatigue mechanisms]] [supported]; [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing|Verkhoshansky taper timing]] [supported]; [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation|Verkhoshansky adaptive reconstruction]] [contested]; [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle|Bompa supercompensation]] [supported]; [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching|Bompa concentrated loading]] [supported]; [[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept|Evans fitness-fatigue]] [untested].

# Peaking and tapering in an in-season college football schedule

## 1. The question

How should we peak and taper in season? In practice: what a game week looks like as a small taper, how long each quality lasts without exposure, how to read game-week readiness, and what to do in game-free windows (byes, camp to week 1, the postseason gap).

The sources answer a different question. Every peaking model in the library comes from individual-event sports (kayak, swimming, track and field). **External:** Pyne, Mujika and Reilly 2009 (abstract): taper research does not yet guide a team's league season. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 5): sustaining a peak across a long season is unrealistic. No study in two periodization meta-analyses tested whether adaptations peaked when predicted ([[research-papers/afonso-2019-a-systematic-review-of-meta-analyses-comparing-periodized-and-non-periodized-exercise-prog|Afonso 2019]], pp. 1, 4). So the season is "hold readiness weekly"; "peak on purpose" is for game-free windows.

## 2. Bottom line

1. Every game week keeps two floors: one heavy lower-body session, load high, sets cut [supported direction; the tested minimum, not Issurin's two-session template; no football trial], and one planned max-velocity exposure [contested; no football data]. Inference: prioritize positions that rarely reach top speed in games (untested).
2. Lift heaviest early; for a Saturday game, the last high-volume practice falls no later than Wednesday, and volume, not intensity, drops from Thursday. [Issurin's template (rugby league) and one D-I program agree on early-heavy, late-light but differ on the heaviest practice day; descriptive only] Inference: about 48 h from the last heavy session to kickoff, drawn from Verkhoshansky's 48 h recovery after high-CNS work and Pritchard 2015's 2 to 4 days of cessation before a strength peak; no source tests a gap to kickoff.
3. Read readiness from CMJ strategy metrics (mRSI or RSImod, FT:CT), no arm swing, against each player's norm, not jump height alone or ACWR. They are noisier than jump height, so set thresholds from each player's typical error. [supported direction; small football samples] Inference: position and starter splits rest on off-season profiles and one exploratory study.
4. Keep aerobic and repeat-effort conditioning every week; it may be lost fastest. [contested: Eric's baseline and Mujika and Padilla 2000 against Issurin's table]
5. Save a real taper (about 1 to 3 weeks, volume cut about 40 to 60%, intensity kept) for one peak after a game-free gap, such as a bowl. [supported in other sports; untested in football]

## 3. Where the sources agree

**Cut volume, keep intensity.** Issurin's pre-competitive microcycle cuts volume, keeps frequency and raises the max-speed share ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning|Issurin pre-competitive]] [supported], PDF p. 105). **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003 (abstract): volume down 60 to 90%, frequency down no more than 20%, intensity kept. **External:** Bosquet et al. 2007 (abstract; 27 studies, sports not listed, mostly endurance per the evidence file): 2 weeks, volume down 41 to 60%. **External:** Pritchard et al. 2019 (abstract; 11 strength-trained men, 1-week taper, about 70% volume cut): tapers did not differ significantly; only the higher-intensity one showed small effect-size gains in IMTP and CMJ FT:CT.

**Strength holds on a small dose.** Issurin, citing Fleck and Kraemer, says team-sport players hold strength 14 to 16 weeks ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle|Issurin in-season]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-109). **External:** Ronnestad et al. 2011 (abstract; pro soccer, n = 7 per group): one session a week kept strength and 40-m sprint for 12 weeks, one every two weeks lost both, and jump height did not change in either group. **External:** Spiering et al. 2021 (abstract; mostly younger non-athletes) agree, with data too thin for athletes.

**Heavy early, light late.** Issurin, citing Baker 2001 (rugby league), lifts Tuesday and Wednesday mornings, holds the week's key practice ("substantial or big" load) Thursday afternoon, and restricts only the pre-game session, for a Sunday game (Issurin in-season, PDF pp. 108-111). Inference: for a Saturday game, lifts move to Monday and Tuesday and key practice to Wednesday. **External:** Wellman et al. 2019 (31 D-I players, one program, PDF p. 6): late-season Tuesday and Wednesday loads fell by a planned duration cut; Thursday did not change.

**Strategy metrics beat output.** Jump height fell only slightly by 24 h while RSImod and FT:CT stayed largely reduced ([[research-papers/lewis-undated-athlete-monitoring-in-american-collegiate-football|Lewis]], pp. 96-97; D-I, n = 5). At 72 h, flight time moved -0.7% and FT:CT -7.7% ([[research-papers/gathercole-2015-alternative-countermovement-jump-analysis-to-quantify-acute-neuromuscular-fatigue|Gathercole 2015]], p. 7; n = 8). The cost is noise: several phase and RFD variables failed reliability, FT:CT worse with arm swing ([[research-papers/heishman-2020-countermovement-jump-reliability-performed-with-and-without-an-arm-swing-in-ncaa-division|Heishman 2020]], pp. 5-12). ACWR beat no intercept-only model ([[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor|Impellizzeri 2020]], pp. 4-5).

## 4. Where they disagree

**Heaviest practice day, and the post-game window.** Issurin's key practice is late (Wednesday, shifted). College data put load early: Wellman's Tuesday was the planned highest practice (PDF p. 6); Lewis (PDF p. 86) found Tuesday and Wednesday closest to game demands for linemen. Both sit inside the post-game window: after AFL matches, IMTP RFD (0 to 50 ms) was still down about 17% at 72 and 96 h, CV 16.4% ([[research-papers/norris-2019-recovery-of-forcetime-characteristics-after-australian-rules-football-matches-examining-th|Norris 2019]], p. 2); after soccer, hamstring RTD and sprint were impaired at 72 h ([[research-papers/cosio-2026-transcriptomic-profiling-of-the-biceps-femoris-long-head-72-h-following-a-football-match-a|Cosio 2026]], p. 8; n = 9, no control). After a Saturday game, Monday is about 48 h, Tuesday 72, Wednesday 96. Unresolved: lift on incompletely recovered players by design (Issurin), or hold heavy and high-velocity work until Wednesday. Settle with our CMJ and sprint data by hours since the game.

**Which quality is lost first (D-6).** Issurin: speed first (5 ± 3 days), aerobic and strength last (30 ± 5), no sample ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability|Issurin residuals]] [contested], PDF p. 35). **Eric's baseline (class-4-2026 slides, p. 47):** aerobic first, speed last. **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2000 (abstract): under 4 weeks, trained athletes lose VO2max fast, strength little. Inference: this sides with class 4. **External:** Saldanha et al. 2026 (abstract; 17 to 21 semi-pro soccer players, uncontrolled): after 5 days off, repeated-sprint time and RAST peak velocity worsened while jump and hip adductor and abductor strength held. Inference: leans toward Issurin, though RAST is not a max-velocity test. Against: **External:** Ross and Leveritt 2001 (PDF p. 17): short-sprint detraining is "less severe than may have been reasonably anticipated". **External:** Bosquet et al. 2013 (abstract; 103 studies): cessation cut maximal power least (SMD -0.20). Ronnestad kept sprint without dedicated max-velocity work. The residual entry notes these may measure cessation versus a retention dose, and Issurin calls residual-only design "extremely rigid and inflexible" ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks|Issurin mini-blocks]] [supported], PDF p. 127). Settle with our sprint and CMJ data around byes and winter break.

**Heavy lifting near competition (D-5, D-7).** Platonov and Fesenko say it hurts technique; Bompa and Carrera say it keeps force (Issurin pre-competitive, PDF p. 108). **External:** Pritchard et al. 2015 (abstract): 2 to 4 days of training cessation looks optimal for peak strength. Inference: a football week never stops, so this bounds the last heavy lift; the shifted Issurin week puts it about 4 days out.

**Maintain or build.** **External:** Ronnestad and Spiering maintain on one session; Issurin uses two. **External:** Hoffman et al. 2003 (abstract; freshmen, n = 14 per group, 2 sessions a week): the linear program raised 1RM squat 13.8 ± 7.4 kg, the nonlinear did not; the abstract garbles one program. Inference: building may suit low-snap freshmen, not starters.

**Timing models.** Bompa ([[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle|Bompa supercompensation]] [supported]), Verkhoshansky ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation|Verkhoshansky reconstruction]] [contested]) and Evans ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept|Evans fitness-fatigue]] [untested]) disagree on whether adaptation timing is predictable. Inference: mental models, not a clock.

## 5. What transfers and what does not

**Transfers:** residual direction and weekly re-exposure; the two-mini-block week as a template; keep intensity, cut volume; CMJ strategy metrics. Body mass is not a taper marker: fat mass rose 4.3% over a 2-week taper at stable mass ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription|Issurin realization]] [supported], PDF pp. 126-127; triathletes, n = 16, untested for significance). Inference: linemen eating heavily in a low-load window are most exposed.

**Does not transfer:** single-peak prescriptions (1 to 3 week realization, kayak dosages, 4 to 12 week delayed gains per Siff and Verkhoshansky cited by Bompa ([[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching|Bompa loading]] [supported]), the 3% taper gain) assume one target event.

**The exception, a bowl.** **External:** Marrier et al. 2017 (abstract; 10 rugby sevens players, 3-week taper): 70 to 80% of peaks fell in the first 2 weeks. **External:** Vachon et al. 2021 (abstract; 14 team-sport studies): moderate gains in power, change of direction and VO2max; no best strategy. **External:** Haugen et al. 2019 (PDF p. 11): 2 to 3 weeks for strength and power sports; smaller gains in sprinters. Fitz-Clarke 1991 finds usual tapers "may be too rigorous and short" ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing|Verkhoshansky taper]] [supported]). Inference: 1 to 3 weeks of reduced volume, speed and heavy lifting kept, not judged by sprint times alone.

## 6. What none of them covers

- **Bye weeks.** **External:** Peterson (dissertation, unverified year; 108 D-I players) found a group x time interaction on a CMJ stretch-shortening factor: the gap between big and skill or mid-size players widened after the bye and lasted 24 h past the next game (PDF p. 52). Within-group change is not tested there. Inference: dose byes by position and keep a speed or repeated-sprint exposure, given Saldanha.
- **Short weeks, camp to week 1, position groups, low-snap players.** Only descriptive or off-population data: soccer load ratios ([[research-papers/galiano-2026-more-matches-less-time-how-load-ratios-reveal-gaps-between-training-and-competition-in-foo|Galiano 2026]]), U17 futsal ([[research-papers/claudino-2016-autoregulating-jump-performance-to-induce-functional-overreaching|Claudino 2016]]), off-season CMJ by position ([[research-papers/merrigan-2022-comparisons-of-countermovement-jump-force-time-characteristics-among-national-collegiate-a|Merrigan 2022]]), game load by exposure ([[research-papers/lever-2026-game-exposure-shapes-intensity-and-performance-in-division-i-college-football|Lever 2026]]), non-starters recovering worse on lower load ([[research-papers/aychman-2026-multimodal-indicators-of-non-functional-overreaching-in-ncaa-division-i-american-football|Aychman 2026]], pp. 1, 9; one program, exploratory).
- **Postseason and playoffs.** Bowl structure is Inference from kayak calendars; after a long layoff, rebuild contact over 3 to 4 weeks ([[research-papers/stokes-2020-returning-to-play-after-prolonged-training-restrictions-in-professional-collision-sports|Stokes 2020]], p. 7; expert opinion).
- **Season-long detraining.** Only the 14 to 16 week figure and Hoffman 2003 (freshman strength); nothing on starters' speed.

Would fill: Bompa Ch 7, Issurin Ch 4; others in the evidence map, Gaps.

## 7. Eric's baseline

- **Eric's baseline:** daily CMJ mRSI is the readiness marker, "objective, consistent, and actionable" (SportSmith piece); wellness surveys were dropped after athletes gamed them. Inference: this matches section 3 and [[research-papers/mccall-2023-a-qualitative-study-of-11-world-class-team-sport-athletes-experiences-answering-subjective|McCall 2023]].
- **Eric's baseline (class-4-2026 slides, p. 47):** aerobic traits are lost fastest, speed slowest; that order sets re-exposure. This conflicts with Issurin.
- **Course baseline (HHPR 5355, speaker unconfirmed):** speed every 5 days, aerobic and max strength every 30 (class-1 p. 27). These are Issurin's Table 1.6 reproduced in the slides (week1-lecture p. 66), not independent support, and class-1 also says aerobic is gained and lost quickly (pp. 25, 28). The real disagreement is class-4 p. 47 against Issurin.
- **Course baseline (HHPR 5355, speaker unconfirmed):** "maintain intensity, reduce volume", a strength retention dose, a waved week not tied to 7 days (class-1 pp. 17-25; class-8 p. 21). Agrees with section 3.
- **Eric's baseline (class-4 slides, pp. 34, 39):** conditioning targets alactic and aerobic capacity; glycolytic work comes through practice. Inference: fits the 1:7 ratio in 2004 D-I games ([[research-papers/iosia-2008-analysis-of-exercise-to-rest-ratios-during-division-ia-televised-football-competition|Iosia 2008]]).

## 8. Questions for Eric

1. In a 12-plus game season, does "peak" mean every Saturday, target games, or only the postseason?
2. In a Saturday week, where do the heaviest lifts and practice sit now? Issurin's shifted week lifts Monday and Tuesday, 48 and 72 h post-game, when fast force is still down. Deliberate, or should heavy and high-velocity work wait until Wednesday?
3. Class-4 (p. 47) says aerobic is lost fastest; the course's 5 and 30 day figures are Issurin's table, and class-1 says aerobic goes quickly too. Is class-4 your view, and are the course in-season rules yours?
4. How are bye weeks used now: restoration, loading, or a speed and strength top-up, and by position?
5. Which mRSI drop, on which day, changes the plan, and do linemen and low-snap players get their own thresholds?
6. Does the postseason get a distinct 1 to 3 week taper or the normal game-week template?

## 9. Sources used

Library entries (confidence): [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription|Issurin realization]] [supported]; [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning|Issurin pre-competitive]] [supported]; [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability|Issurin residuals]] [contested]; [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle|Issurin in-season]] [supported]; [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks|Issurin mini-blocks]] [supported]; [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms|Verkhoshansky fatigue]] [supported]; [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing|Verkhoshansky taper]] [supported]; [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation|Verkhoshansky reconstruction]] [contested]; [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle|Bompa supercompensation]] [supported]; [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching|Bompa loading]] [supported]; [[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept|Evans fitness-fatigue]] [untested].

Paper briefs: Afonso, Cosio, Norris, Lewis, Gathercole, Heishman, Galiano, Claudino, Stokes, Merrigan, Impellizzeri, Lever, Aychman, McCall, Iosia.

External (labelled in text): Bosquet 2007, 2013; Mujika and Padilla 2000, 2003; Vachon 2021; Marrier 2017; Pritchard 2015, 2019; Haugen 2019; Pyne 2009; Ronnestad 2011; Spiering 2021; Cuthbert 2024; Wellman 2019; Hoffman 2003; Peterson; Ross and Leveritt 2001; Saldanha 2026. # Peaking and tapering in an in-season college football schedule

## 1. The question

How should we peak and taper in season? In practice: what a game week looks like as a small taper, how long each quality lasts without exposure, how to read game-week readiness, and what to do in game-free windows (byes, camp to week 1, the postseason gap).

The sources answer a different question. Every peaking model in the library comes from individual-event sports (kayak, swimming, track and field). **External:** Pyne, Mujika and Reilly 2009 (abstract): taper research does not yet guide a team's league season. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 5): sustaining a peak across a long season is unrealistic. No study in two periodization meta-analyses tested whether adaptations peaked when predicted ([[research-papers/afonso-2019-a-systematic-review-of-meta-analyses-comparing-periodized-and-non-periodized-exercise-prog|Afonso 2019]], pp. 1, 4). So the season is "hold readiness weekly"; "peak on purpose" is for game-free windows.

## 2. Bottom line

1. Every game week keeps two floors: one heavy lower-body session, load high, sets cut [supported direction; the tested minimum, not Issurin's two-session template; no football trial], and one planned max-velocity exposure [contested; no football data]. Inference: prioritize positions that rarely reach top speed in games (untested).
2. Lift heaviest early; for a Saturday game, the last high-volume practice falls no later than Wednesday, and volume, not intensity, drops from Thursday. [Issurin's template (rugby league) and one D-I program agree on early-heavy, late-light but differ on the heaviest practice day; descriptive only] Inference: about 48 h from the last heavy session to kickoff, drawn from Verkhoshansky's 48 h recovery after high-CNS work and Pritchard 2015's 2 to 4 days of cessation before a strength peak; no source tests a gap to kickoff.
3. Read readiness from CMJ strategy metrics (mRSI or RSImod, FT:CT), no arm swing, against each player's norm, not jump height alone or ACWR. They are noisier than jump height, so set thresholds from each player's typical error. [supported direction; small football samples] Inference: position and starter splits rest on off-season profiles and one exploratory study.
4. Keep aerobic and repeat-effort conditioning every week; it may be lost fastest. [contested: Eric's baseline and Mujika and Padilla 2000 against Issurin's table]
5. Save a real taper (about 1 to 3 weeks, volume cut about 40 to 60%, intensity kept) for one peak after a game-free gap, such as a bowl. [supported in other sports; untested in football]

## 2. Bottom line

Every game week has two floors: one heavy lower-body session, load high and sets cut [supported direction; the tested minimum, not Issurin's two-session template; no football trial], and one planned max-velocity exposure for every player [contested; no football data]. Inference: prioritize positions that rarely reach top speed in games (no source tests this).

-2. Lift heaviest early in the week; for a Saturday game, hold the last high-volume practice no later than Wednesday and cut volume, not intensity, from Thursday. [Issurin's template (rugby league, Baker 2001) and one D-I program agree on early-heavy, late-light; they differ on the heaviest practice day; descriptive only in college football] Inference: keep about 48 h between the last heavy or high-volume session and kickoff, drawn from Verkhoshansky's 48 h recovery after high-CNS work and Pritchard 2015's 2 to 4 days of cessation before a strength peak; no source tests a gap to kickoff.

[supported direction; football samples are small] Inference: splitting by position group and starter status rests on off-season profiles and one exploratory study; no source sets game-week thresholds by group.

## 3. Where the sources agree

-**Cut volume, keep intensity.** Issurin's pre-competitive microcycle cuts total and intense volume, keeps session frequency, and raises the share of max-speed and sport-specific work ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning|Issurin pre-competitive]] [supported], PDF p. 105). **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003 (abstract): keep intensity, cut volume up to 60 to 90%, cut frequency no more than 20%. **External:** Bosquet et al. 2007 (abstract; 27 studies; sports not listed in the abstract, mostly endurance per the evidence file): a 2-week taper with volume cut 41 to 60% and no change in intensity or frequency was most efficient. **External:** Pritchard et al. 2019 (abstract; crossover, 11 strength-trained men, 1-week taper, about 70% volume cut): the tapers did not differ significantly; only the higher-intensity taper showed small effect-size gains in IMTP relative peak force and CMJ FT:CT.

+**Cut volume, keep intensity.** Issurin's pre-competitive microcycle cuts volume, keeps frequency and raises the max-speed share ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning|Issurin pre-competitive]] [supported], PDF p. 105). **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003 (abstract): volume down 60 to 90%, frequency down no more than 20%, intensity kept. **External:** Bosquet et al. 2007 (abstract; 27 studies, sports not listed, mostly endurance per the evidence file): 2 weeks, volume down 41 to 60%. **External:** Pritchard et al. 2019 (abstract; 11 strength-trained men, 1-week taper, about 70% volume cut): tapers did not differ significantly; only the higher-intensity one showed small effect-size gains in IMTP and CMJ FT:CT.

-**Strength holds on a small dose.** Issurin, citing Fleck and Kraemer 1997, says team-sport players hold strength near pre-season for 14 to 16 weeks, then lose it sharply ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle|Issurin in-season week]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-109; secondhand). **External:** Ronnestad et al. 2011 (abstract; professional soccer, n = 7 per group): one session per week kept strength and 40-m sprint for 12 weeks; one every two weeks lost both; jump height did not change in either group. **External:** Spiering et al. 2021 (abstract; mostly younger general adults) found strength held up to 32 weeks on one set per exercise per week at kept relative load, but say the data are too thin for athlete advice.

+**Strength holds on a small dose.** Issurin, citing Fleck and Kraemer, says team-sport players hold strength 14 to 16 weeks ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle|Issurin in-season]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-109). **External:** Ronnestad et al. 2011 (abstract; pro soccer, n = 7 per group): one session a week kept strength and 40-m sprint for 12 weeks, one every two weeks lost both, and jump height did not change in either group. **External:** Spiering et al. 2021 (abstract; mostly younger non-athletes) agree, with data too thin for athletes.

-**Heavy early, light late.** Issurin, citing Baker 2001 (one rugby league study), splits the week into an early strength mini-block and a late practice mini-block. Inference: shifting one day earlier for a Saturday game gives lifts Monday and Tuesday mornings, key practice Wednesday afternoon, Thursday off, a light Friday. High volume just before competition may hurt ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing|Verkhoshansky taper timing]] [supported], PDF pp. 99-100). **External:** Wellman et al. 2019 (Zotero; 31 D-I players, one program, PDF p. 6): in weeks 9 to 12 Tuesday and Wednesday loads fell by a preplanned duration cut while Thursday did not change.

Inference: for a Saturday game, lifts move to Monday and Tuesday and key practice to Wednesday. **External:** Wellman et al. 2019 (31 D-I players, one program, PDF p. 6): late-season Tuesday and Wednesday loads fell by a planned duration cut; Thursday did not change.

-**Strategy metrics beat output metrics.** In D-I football, jump height fell only slightly by 24 h after training while RSImod and FT:CT stayed largely reduced ([[research-papers/lewis-undated-athlete-monitoring-in-american-collegiate-football|Lewis]], pp. 96-97; n = 5). ## 4. Where they disagree

-**Where the heaviest practice sits, and the post-game window.** Issurin puts the key practice late (Wednesday after the Saturday shift). College data put it early: Wellman's program planned Tuesday as the highest practice load (PDF p. 6), and Lewis (dissertation, year unverified; PDF p. 86) found Tuesday and Wednesday practices closest to game demands for linemen. Both sit inside the post-game window. After AFL matches, early IMTP RFD (0 to 50 ms) was still down 17.8% at 72 h and 16.9% at 96 h while peak force barely moved, CV 16.4% ([[research-papers/norris-2019-recovery-of-forcetime-characteristics-after-australian-rules-football-matches-examining-th|Norris 2019]], p. 2). After a soccer match, hamstring RTD and sprint time were still impaired at 72 h ([[research-papers/cosio-2026-transcriptomic-profiling-of-the-biceps-femoris-long-head-72-h-following-a-football-match-a|Cosio 2026]], p. 8; n = 9, no control group). A Saturday game puts Monday at about 48 h, Tuesday about 72 h, Wednesday about 96 h. Unresolved: either the early-week lifts and practice load incompletely recovered players by design (Issurin's model), or heavy and high-velocity work waits until Wednesday. No source tests this in football. What would settle it: our CMJ and sprint data by hours since the game.

+**Heaviest practice day, and the post-game window.** Issurin's key practice is late (Wednesday, shifted). College data put load early: Wellman's Tuesday was the planned highest practice (PDF p. 6); Lewis (PDF p. 86) found Tuesday and Wednesday closest to game demands for linemen. Both sit inside the post-game window: after AFL matches, IMTP RFD (0 to 50 ms) was still down about 17% at 72 and 96 h, CV 16.4% ([[research-papers/norris-2019-recovery-of-forcetime-characteristics-after-australian-rules-football-matches-examining-th|Norris 2019]], p. 2); after soccer, hamstring RTD and sprint were impaired at 72 h ([[research-papers/cosio-2026-transcriptomic-profiling-of-the-biceps-femoris-long-head-72-h-following-a-football-match-a|Cosio 2026]], p. 8; n = 9, no control). After a Saturday game, Monday is about 48 h, Tuesday 72, Wednesday 96. Unresolved: lift on incompletely recovered players by design (Issurin), or hold heavy and high-velocity work until Wednesday. Settle with our CMJ and sprint data by hours since the game.

# Peaking and tapering in an in-season college football schedule

## 1. The question

How should we peak and taper in season? In practice: what a game week looks like as a small taper, how long each quality lasts unexposed, how to read game-week readiness, and what to do in game-free windows (byes, camp to week 1, the postseason).

The sources answer a different question. Every peaking model in the library comes from individual-event sports (kayak, swimming, track and field). **External:** Pyne, Mujika and Reilly 2009 (abstract): taper research does not yet guide a team's league season. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 5): a season-long peak is unrealistic. No study in two periodization meta-analyses tested whether adaptations peaked when predicted ([[research-papers/afonso-2019-a-systematic-review-of-meta-analyses-comparing-periodized-and-non-periodized-exercise-prog|Afonso 2019]], pp. 1, 4). So: hold readiness weekly, and peak on purpose only in game-free windows.

## 2. Bottom line

1. Every game week keeps one heavy lower-body session, load high, sets cut [supported direction; the tested minimum, not Issurin's two-session template; no football trial], and one planned max-velocity exposure [contested; no football data]. Inference: prioritize positions that rarely reach top speed in games.
2. Lift heaviest early; for a Saturday game the last high-volume practice falls by Wednesday, and volume, not intensity, drops from Thursday. [Issurin (rugby league) and one D-I program agree on early-heavy, late-light but differ on the heaviest practice day; descriptive only] Inference: about 48 h from the last heavy session to kickoff, from Verkhoshansky's 48 h recovery after high-CNS work and Pritchard 2015's 2 to 4 days of cessation before a strength peak; untested.
3. Read readiness from CMJ strategy metrics (mRSI or RSImod, FT:CT), no arm swing, against each player's norm, not jump height alone or ACWR. They are noisier, so set thresholds from each player's typical error. [supported direction; small football samples] Inference: position and starter splits rest on off-season profiles and one exploratory study.
4. Keep aerobic and repeat-effort conditioning every week; it may be lost fastest. [contested: Eric's baseline and Mujika and Padilla 2000 against Issurin]
5. Save a real taper (about 1 to 3 weeks, volume down 40 to 60%, intensity kept) for one peak after a game-free gap, such as a bowl. [supported in other sports; untested in football]

## 3. Where the sources agree

**Cut volume, keep intensity.** Issurin's pre-competitive week cuts volume, keeps frequency and raises the max-speed share ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning|Issurin pre-competitive]] [supported], PDF p. 105). **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003 (abstract): volume down 60 to 90%, frequency down at most 20%. **External:** Bosquet et al. 2007 (abstract; 27 studies, mostly endurance per the evidence file): 2 weeks, volume down 41 to 60%. **External:** Pritchard et al. 2019 (abstract; 11 strength-trained men, 1-week taper, about 70% volume cut): tapers did not differ significantly; only the higher-intensity one showed small effect-size gains in IMTP and FT:CT.

**Strength holds on a small dose.** Issurin, citing Fleck and Kraemer, says team-sport players hold strength 14 to 16 weeks ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle|Issurin in-season]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-109). **External:** Ronnestad et al. 2011 (abstract; pro soccer, n = 7 per group): one session a week kept strength and 40-m sprint for 12 weeks; one every two weeks lost both; jump height did not change in either group. **External:** Spiering et al. 2021 (abstract; mostly non-athletes) agrees.

**Heavy early, light late.** For a Sunday game, Issurin (citing Baker 2001, rugby league) lifts Tuesday and Wednesday mornings, holds the key practice ("substantial or big" load) Thursday afternoon, and restricts only the pre-game session (Issurin in-season, PDF pp. 108-111). Inference: for Saturday, lifts move to Monday and Tuesday, key practice to Wednesday. **External:** Wellman et al. 2019 (31 D-I players, one program, PDF p. 6): late-season Tuesday and Wednesday loads fell by a planned duration cut; Thursday did not change.

**Strategy metrics beat output.** Jump height fell only slightly by 24 h while RSImod and FT:CT stayed down ([[research-papers/lewis-undated-athlete-monitoring-in-american-collegiate-football|Lewis]], pp. 96-97; n = 5). At 72 h, flight time moved -0.7% and FT:CT -7.7% ([[research-papers/gathercole-2015-alternative-countermovement-jump-analysis-to-quantify-acute-neuromuscular-fatigue|Gathercole 2015]], p. 7; n = 8). The cost is noise: several phase and RFD variables failed reliability ([[research-papers/heishman-2020-countermovement-jump-reliability-performed-with-and-without-an-arm-swing-in-ncaa-division|Heishman 2020]], pp. 5-12). ACWR did no better than an intercept-only model ([[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor|Impellizzeri 2020]], pp. 4-5).

## 4. Where they disagree

**Heaviest practice day, and the post-game window.** Issurin's key practice is late (Wednesday, shifted). Wellman's program planned Tuesday as its highest practice (PDF p. 6); Lewis (PDF p. 86) found Tuesday and Wednesday closest to game demands for linemen. Both sit in the post-game window: after AFL matches, IMTP RFD (0 to 50 ms) was still down about 17% at 72 and 96 h, CV 16.4% ([[research-papers/norris-2019-recovery-of-forcetime-characteristics-after-australian-rules-football-matches-examining-th|Norris 2019]], p. 2); after soccer, hamstring RTD and sprint were impaired at 72 h ([[research-papers/cosio-2026-transcriptomic-profiling-of-the-biceps-femoris-long-head-72-h-following-a-football-match-a|Cosio 2026]], p. 8; n = 9, no control). After Saturday, Monday is about 48 h, Tuesday 72, Wednesday 96. Unresolved: lift on incompletely recovered players by design (Issurin), or hold heavy and high-velocity work until Wednesday. Settle with our CMJ and sprint data by hours since the game.

**Which quality goes first (D-6).** Issurin: speed (5 ± 3 days) before aerobic and strength (30 ± 5), no sample ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability|Issurin residuals]] [contested], PDF p. 35). **Eric's baseline (class-4-2026 slides, p. 47):** aerobic first, speed last. **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2000 (abstract): within 4 weeks, trained athletes lose VO2max fast, strength little. Inference: this sides with class 4. **External:** Saldanha et al. 2026 (abstract; 17 to 21 semi-pro soccer players, uncontrolled): after 5 days off, repeated-sprint time and RAST peak velocity worsened; jump and hip adductor and abductor strength held. Inference: leans toward Issurin, though RAST is not a max-velocity test. Against: **External:** Ross and Leveritt 2001 (PDF p. 17): short-sprint detraining is "less severe than may have been reasonably anticipated". **External:** Bosquet et al. 2013 (abstract; 103 studies): cessation cut maximal power least. Ronnestad kept sprint without max-velocity work. The residual entry notes these may measure cessation versus a retention dose; Issurin calls residual-only design "extremely rigid and inflexible" ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks|Issurin mini-blocks]] [supported], PDF p. 127). Settle with our data around byes and winter break.

**Lifting near competition (D-5, D-7).** Platonov and Fesenko say it hurts technique; Bompa and Carrera say it keeps force (Issurin pre-competitive, PDF p. 108). **External:** Pritchard et al. 2015 (abstract): 2 to 4 days of training cessation looks optimal for peak strength. Inference: football never stops training, so this only bounds the last lift; the shifted Issurin week puts it 4 days out.

**Maintain or build.** Ronnestad and Spiering maintain on one session; Issurin uses two. **External:** Hoffman et al. 2003 (abstract; freshmen, n = 14 per group, 2 sessions a week): a linear program raised 1RM squat 13.8 ± 7.4 kg, a nonlinear one did not; the abstract garbles one program. Inference: building may suit low-snap freshmen, not starters.

**Timing models.** [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle|Bompa]] [supported], [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation|Verkhoshansky]] [contested] and [[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept|Evans]] [untested] disagree on whether adaptation timing is predictable. Inference: mental models, not a clock.

## 5. What transfers and what does not

**Transfers:** residual direction and weekly re-exposure; the two-mini-block week as a template; keep intensity, cut volume; CMJ strategy metrics. Body mass is not a taper marker: fat mass rose 4.3% at stable mass over 2 weeks ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription|Issurin realization]] [supported], PDF pp. 126-127; triathletes, n = 16, no significance test).

- **Postseason.** Bowl structure is Inference from kayak calendars; after a long layoff, rebuild contact over 3 to 4 weeks ([[research-papers/stokes-2020-returning-to-play-after-prolonged-training-restrictions-in-professional-collision-sports|Stokes 2020]], p. 7; expert opinion).

Would fill: Bompa Ch 7, Issurin Ch 4; others in the evidence map, Gaps.
